name: Gestalt proximity
definition: Nearby visual elements tend to be perceived as belonging together.

name: Gestalt similarity
definition: Elements sharing visual properties tend to be perceptually grouped.

name: Visual discrimination
definition: The ability to distinguish differences in visual properties such as position, length, colour or shape.

name: Spatial perception
definition: Perception and interpretation of spatial relationships between visual elements.

name: Visual search
definition: The process of locating target information among competing visual items.

name: Selective attention
definition: Prioritising task-relevant information while suppressing competing information.

name: Attentional capture
definition: Automatic redirection of attention toward salient or unexpected visual elements.

name: Change blindness
definition: Failure to notice changes when visual continuity is disrupted or attention is elsewhere.

name: Working memory
definition: Limited-capacity maintenance and manipulation of information during a task.

name: Visual working memory
definition: Temporary maintenance of visual features and spatial relationships.

name: Chunking
definition: Grouping elements into meaningful units to reduce memory demands.

name: Recognition vs recall
definition: Recognising visible information is often less demanding than retrieving it from memory.

name: Cognitive load
definition: The mental resources required to process, integrate and reason about information.

name: Mental models
definition: Internal representations used to understand systems, concepts or relationships.

name: Spatial reasoning
definition: Reasoning using spatial arrangements, distances and relationships.

name: Categorisation
definition: Assigning items to conceptual groups or classes based on perceived evidence.

name: Anchoring
definition: Judgements can be biased toward an initial reference point.

name: Framing
definition: Equivalent information can produce different judgements depending on how it is presented.

name: Risk perception
definition: Subjective interpretation of the magnitude and likelihood of potential outcomes.

name: Probability judgement
definition: Estimation and interpretation of likelihood under uncertainty.

name: Preattentive processing
definition: Rapid detection of certain visual properties, such as colour, orientation, size or motion, before focused attention is engaged.

name: Signal detection theory
definition: Discrimination of meaningful signals from noise under uncertainty, shaped by both perceptual sensitivity and decision criteria.

name: Perceptual thresholds
definition: Weber–Fechner and just-noticeable-difference principles describing how large a visual change must be to become detectable.

name: Feature integration theory
definition: Basic visual features are processed in parallel, while focused attention helps bind multiple features into coherent objects.

name: Broadbent’s filter model
definition: A limited-capacity attentional filter selects some information for further processing while other competing input is attenuated or excluded.

name: Dual-coding theory
definition: Information represented through coordinated verbal and visual systems may support comprehension and later retrieval.

name: Conceptual mapping
definition: Spatial or visual structures can map abstract conceptual relationships into forms that support reasoning and comparison.

name: Embodied cognition
definition: Cognition is shaped by bodily action, spatial experience and interaction with the environment.

name: Distributed cognition
definition: Cognitive activity is distributed across people, representations, tools and the surrounding environment.

name: Sensemaking theory
definition: People iteratively organise, interpret and externalise information to construct plausible accounts of complex situations.

name: Dual-process theory
definition: Judgement can involve fast, intuitive processing and slower, more deliberative reasoning, with different vulnerabilities and strengths.

name: Heuristics and biases
definition: People use simplifying judgement strategies that can produce systematic effects such as availability, anchoring and framing biases.

name: Emotional design theory
definition: Aesthetic and affective qualities of an interface can influence engagement, perceived usability and interpretation.

name: Affect–cognition interaction
definition: Emotional responses and anticipated feelings can influence attention, interpretation, risk perception and decision-making.

name: Elaboration likelihood model
definition: Persuasion can follow a central route based on careful evaluation or a peripheral route based on cues requiring less elaboration.

name: Attitude and behaviour change
definition: Message framing, credibility, norms and perceived relevance can influence attitudes, intentions and behaviour.

name: Ecological perception
definition: Perception is understood in relation to meaningful environmental structure, context and possibilities for action.

name: Multimedia learning theory
definition: Learning from coordinated words and pictures depends on limited processing capacity, active integration and management of extraneous material.

name: Constructivist learning
definition: Learners actively construct understanding by connecting new representations with prior knowledge, experience and interpretation.

name: External representations
definition: Visual and interactive representations can store, reorganise and expose information in ways that change the cognitive work required.

name: Human information processing
definition: A broad account of information moving through perceptual, attentional, memory and decision processes with capacity and selection constraints.
